extracted.intended_audience: current and prospective peer reviewers for The BMJ (including patient reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and requirements for peer reviewers working for The BMJ, including procedural expectations, open peer review policy, declaration of competing interests, and evaluation priorities (originality, importance, reliability, and relevance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign reports and declare competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: We ask reviewers to sign their reports and declare any competing interests on any manuscripts we send them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to all manuscripts sent to reviewers for The BMJ; declarations of competing interests should accompany the signed report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers advise editors; editors make the final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers advise the editors, who make the final decision (aided by an editorial manuscript committee meeting for some articles, including original research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers provide assessments and recommendations, but editorial staff (sometimes with a manuscript committee) take responsibility for acceptance/rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review policy for research papers
rubrics_metrics.description: For research papers, The BMJ has fully open peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every accepted research paper submitted from September 2014 onwards will have its prepublication history posted alongside it on thebmj.com.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepublication history components
rubrics_metrics.description: The prepublication history comprises all previous versions of the manuscript, the study protocol, the report from the manuscript committee meeting, the reviewers’ signed comments, and the authors’ responses to all the comments from reviewers and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items are published alongside accepted research papers so readers can see the review history and authors' responses (see editorial for more details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Study protocol submission requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting the protocol is mandatory for all clinical trials and encouraged for all other studies at The BMJ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protocol submission becomes part of the prepublication history; mandatory for clinical trials to promote transparency and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise manuscripts by BMJ aims: originality, importance, reliability, usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: We ask reviewers to help us prioritise the manuscripts that we receive, bearing in mind that The BMJ aims to publish original, important, and reliable articles that will help our readers around the world—who are mainly doctors—to make better decisions about practice, policy, education, and research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a manuscript, reviewers should consider whether it meets these aims and how useful it will be to The BMJ readership; note that all research in The BMJ is published with open access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive critique that assesses importance and originality
rubrics_metrics.description: For the best reviews (those that constructively critique the article and help editors assess its importance and originality) we offer, in partnership with the Cleveland Clinic Foundation, up to 3 AMA PRA Category 1 Continuing Medical Education (CME) points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality reviews are constructive, help editors judge importance/originality, and may be eligible for CME credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient reviewers assess importance and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to peer review, we also ask patient reviewers for their opinion on the importance and relevance of selected manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patient reviewers are asked to focus on the manuscript's importance and relevance from a patient or public perspective; used selectively for certain submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to review invitation via the online editorial office
rubrics_metrics.description: If we need your help with appraising a manuscript we will email you and ask you to accept or reject the reviewing invitation at our online editorial office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should promptly accept or decline invitations through the journal's online system to help editorial workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers usually see at least two reports and can access each other's reports after decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts sent for review are usually seen by at least two reviewers, and reviewers can access each other's reports on the same manuscript once The BMJ has made its decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access to other reviewers' reports is provided after the editorial decision to facilitate feedback and learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article provenance statement (disclose commissioning and peer review status)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of every accepted editorial, research article, clinical review, practice article, analysis article, feature, and head-to-head article The BMJ will add a statement explaining the article's provenance. The options are: Not commissioned; externally peer reviewed; Not commissioned; not externally peer reviewed; Commissioned; externally peer reviewed; Commissioned; not externally peer reviewed; Commissioned, based on an idea from the author; externally peer reviewed; Commissioned, based on an idea from the author; not externally peer reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provenance statement makes clear whether the article was commissioned and whether it underwent external peer review; reviewers should be aware that this disclosure will appear on accepted articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use BMJ transparency policy for ethics/plagiarism/fraud concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ transparency policy pulls together in one place many separate editorial policies. It's there, for example, that you'll find advice on what to do if you are concerned about the ethics aspects of a manuscript we have asked you to review or if you suspect plagiarism, duplicate publication, or scientific fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers who have ethical concerns or suspect misconduct should consult the BMJ transparency policy for recommended actions and contact points.
